fuller.text: This paper introduces dropout, a simple trick for training neural networks: computer programs built from many small connected units that learn patterns from examples. Its target is overfitting, where a network learns quirks of its training examples that do not hold for new data. The authors test the trick on vision, speech, text and biology problems.

sentences.text: This paper introduces dropout, a simple trick for training neural networks: computer programs built from many small connected units that learn patterns from examples.
Its target is overfitting, where a network learns quirks of its training examples that do not hold for new data.
The authors test the trick on vision, speech, text and biology problems.

fuller.text: The authors note that averaging the answers of many different models nearly always improves results. But training many separate large networks is very costly, and running them all on new data can be too slow. The ideal would be to average every possible version of a network, weighted by how well each fits the data, but that takes far too much computing. Dropout aims to get close to that ideal far more cheaply.

fuller.text: During training, units are switched off at random, along with their connections, afresh for each training example. Each unit is kept with a probability p, often 0.5 for hidden units and nearer 1 for the input units. So each pass trains a different "thinned" network, a smaller version that shares its connection strengths, called weights, with all the others. When the trained network is used on new data, nothing is switched off; instead each unit's outgoing weights are multiplied by p. This single network stands in for an average of all the thinned networks.

fuller.text: The authors compare this to sexual reproduction, which breaks up sets of genes that only work well together. Likewise, a unit that cannot count on any partner being present must learn something useful on its own. Pictures of what units learned from handwritten digits support this: without dropout, single units looked meaningless, while with dropout they picked out edges, strokes and spots. Dropout also made the network sparse, meaning only a few units responded strongly to each input.

fuller.text: On image tasks, dropout cut error rates, the share of wrong answers, every time. On MNIST, a set of handwritten digits, error fell from about 1.60% to 0.95% with a very large dropout network. On CIFAR-10, small photos in 10 categories, error fell from 14.98% to 12.61%; on CIFAR-100, with 100 categories, it fell from 43.48% to 37.20%. On ImageNet, a contest with 1000 categories, a dropout network won with about 16% top-five error, meaning the right label missed its five best guesses, against about 26% for other methods.

fuller.text: Gains elsewhere were real but varied. On TIMIT speech recordings, the share of wrongly identified speech sounds fell from 23.4% to 21.8%. On sorting Reuters news articles into 50 topics, error fell only from 31.05% to 29.62%. The authors suggest this data set is big enough that overfitting is not a serious problem there.

fuller.text: On a small genetics data set, Bayesian neural networks, which weight each model by how well it fits, scored 623 against dropout's 567, where higher is better. Dropout still beat a standard network, which scored 440, and every other method tried. With only 100 or 500 digit examples, dropout gave no improvement at all. Averaging about 50 randomly thinned networks matched the cheap weight-scaling shortcut, suggesting the shortcut is a fairly good approximation.

fuller.text: The main drawback is time: a dropout network usually takes 2 to 3 times longer to train, because its updates are very noisy. For simple straight-line models, the authors show dropout's average effect equals a known penalty on large weights, but no such shortcut is clear for deeper networks. They conclude that dropout is a general technique, not tied to one field, and that dropout methods hold top results on MNIST, CIFAR-100, ImageNet and another image benchmark.

brief.text: This paper presents dropout, a trick for training neural networks, which are computer programs that learn from examples. Big networks often suffer from overfitting: they memorize their practice examples instead of learning rules that work on new ones. The paper calls this a serious problem, and the usual fix of combining many big networks is too slow.

brief.text: During training, dropout randomly switches off parts of the network, so no part can lean on the others. Afterward, one full network with weakened connections stands in for all those smaller versions. It cut mistakes on pictures, speech, text and genetics, so the authors suggest it is a general technique.
